isle-of-man.title: Isle of Man TT
isle-of-man.summary: The main international event associated with the island is the Isle of Man Tourist Trophy race, colloquially known as "The TT", which began in 1907. Taking place over a two-week period, it has become a festival for motorcycling culture, makes a huge contribution to the island's economy and has become part of Manx identity.

isle-of-man.title: Spuds and herrin
isle-of-man.summary: Traditionally the national dish of the island is "spuds and herrin", boiled potatoes and herring. This plain dish is chosen because of its role supporting the subsistence farmers of the island, who crofted the land and fished the sea for centuries.

fair-isle.title: Fair Isle knitting
fair-isle.summary: Fair Isle (/fɛəraɪ̯l/) is a traditional knitting style used to create patterns with multiple colours. It is named after Fair Isle, one of the Shetland Islands.

During this event young girls and boys dressed in dark jackets play the part of the horses, and young boys using miniature ploughs compete with one another at ploughing a 4-foot square rig in the nearby sands.

jersey.title: Clameur de Haro
jersey.summary: The clameur de haro (French pronunciation: [klamœʁ də aʁo]) is an ancient legal injunction of restraint employed by a person who believes they are being wronged by another at that moment. It survives as a fully enforceable law to this day in the legal systems of Jersey and Guernsey, and is used, albeit infrequently, for matters affecting land.

jersey.title: Visite du Branchage
jersey.summary: Annual visites du branchage are carried out twice in summer by parish officials to inspect roadside verges and hedges and ensure property owners have trimmed back overhanging greenery. This custom is to prevent Jersey's narrow lanes becoming hazardous or impassable through overgrown vegetation.

jersey.title: Tall Jacks

lewis-and-harris.title: Harris Tweed
lewis-and-harris.summary: Harris tweed (Scottish Gaelic: Clò mór or Clò hearach) is a tweed cloth that is handwoven by islanders at their homes in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland, finished in the Outer Hebrides, and made from pure virgin wool dyed and spun in the Outer Hebrides. This definition, quality standards and protection of the Harris tweed name are enshrined in the Harris Tweed Act 1993.

This definition, quality standards and protection of the Harris tweed name are enshrined in the Harris Tweed Act 1993.

lewis-and-harris.title: The guga hunt
lewis-and-harris.summary: In 2018, BBC Alba aired Sulasgeir: An t-Sealg/The Hunt, a Gaelic-language documentary about the traditional annual guga hunt held on Sulasgeir by members of the community of Ness on Lewis.
lewis-and-harris.tie: In 2018, BBC Alba aired Sulasgeir: An t-Sealg/The Hunt, a Gaelic-language documentary about the traditional annual guga hunt held on Sulasgeir by members of the community of Ness on Lewis.

lewis-and-harris.title: Hebridean Celtic Festival
lewis-and-harris.summary: The Hebridean Celtic Festival (Scottish Gaelic: Fèis Cheilteach Innse Gall) or HebCelt is an international Scottish music festival, which takes place annually in Stornoway on Lewis, in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland. The festival regularly attracts over 16,000 attendees and provides significant economic and cultural benefits for its host area.
lewis-and-harris.tie: The Hebridean Celtic Festival (Scottish Gaelic: Fèis Cheilteach Innse Gall) or HebCelt is an international Scottish music festival, which takes place annually in Stornoway on Lewis, in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland. The festival regularly attracts over 16,000 attendees and provides significant economic and cultural benefits for its host area.

osm-relation-380670.title: Harris Tweed
osm-relation-380670.summary: When this trade mark, the Orb, was eventually granted, the board insisted that it should be granted to all the islands of the Outer Hebrides i.e. to Lewis, North and South Uist, Benbecula and Barra, as well as to Harris, the rationale for this decision being that the tweed was made in exactly the same way in all those islands.

osm-relation-380646.title: Fèis Bharraigh
osm-relation-380646.summary: Fèis Bharraigh (Scottish Gaelic pronunciation: [ˌfeːʃˈvarˠaj]) is an annual Gaelic arts and culture event, held on Barra.
osm-relation-380646.tie: Fèis Bharraigh (Scottish Gaelic pronunciation: [ˌfeːʃˈvarˠaj]) is an annual Gaelic arts and culture event, held on Barra.

osm-way-20594001.title: The guga hunt
osm-way-20594001.summary: How long before 1549 the Nessmen sailed to Sula Sgeir each year to collect the young gannets for food and feathers is not known, but it may be assumed that it was a tradition for centuries.
osm-way-20594001.tie: How long before 1549 the Nessmen sailed to Sula Sgeir each year to collect the young gannets for food and feathers is not known, but it may be assumed that it was a tradition for centuries.

st-kilda.title: St Kilda parliament
st-kilda.summary: Another important aspect of St Kildan life was the daily "parliament". This was a meeting held in the street every morning after prayers and attended by all the adult males during the course of which they would decide upon the day's activities.
st-kilda.tie: Another important aspect of St Kildan life was the daily "parliament". This was a meeting held in the street every morning after prayers and attended by all the adult males during the course of which they would decide upon the day's activities.

st-kilda.title: St Kilda mailboat
st-kilda.summary: Even in the late 19th century, the islanders could communicate with the rest of the world only by lighting a bonfire on the summit of Conachair which would, weather permitting, be visible to those on the isles of Harris and the Uists, or by using the "St Kilda mailboat".
st-kilda.tie: Even in the late 19th century, the islanders could communicate with the rest of the world only by lighting a bonfire on the summit of Conachair which would, weather permitting, be visible to those on the isles of Harris and the Uists, or by using the "St Kilda mailboat".

islay.title: Fèis Ìle
islay.summary: Islay is a centre of "whisky tourism", and hosts a "Festival of Malt and Music" known as Fèis Ìle each year on the last week of May, with events and tastings celebrating the cultural heritage of the island.
islay.tie: Islay is a centre of "whisky tourism", and hosts a "Festival of Malt and Music" known as Fèis Ìle each year on the last week of May, with events and tastings celebrating the cultural heritage of the island.

osm-relation-3414078.title: Omey races
osm-relation-3414078.summary: The beach is the site of the annual Omey Races, reestablished in 2001. This horse racing event is held in late summer (July/August).
osm-relation-3414078.tie: The beach is the site of the annual Omey Races, reestablished in 2001. This horse racing event is held in late summer (July/August).

osm-relation-10323151.title: Davaar cave painting
osm-relation-10323151.summary: The island is also known for its seven caves, one of which contains a life-size cave painting depicting the Crucifixion, painted in 1887 by local artist Archibald MacKinnon after he had a vision in a dream suggesting that he do so. The painting caused uproar in the area as it was seen as a sign from God; it is said that when the townsfolk discovered it was MacKinnon, and not God, he was exiled from the town indefinitely.
osm-relation-10323151.tie: The island is also known for its seven caves, one of which contains a life-size cave painting depicting the Crucifixion, painted in 1887 by local artist Archibald MacKinnon after he had a vision in a dream suggesting that he do so. The painting caused uproar in the area as it was seen as a sign from God; it is said that when the townsfolk discovered it was MacKinnon, and not God, he was exiled…

osm-relation-3833751.title: Tigh an Truish
osm-relation-3833751.summary: The well-known pub Tigh an Truish (Gaelic for 'house of the trousers') at Clachan Seil is said to have obtained its name in the wake of the 1745 Jacobite Rebellion. Supposedly, shore-going islanders swapped their kilts for trousers here after Highland dress was banned.

osm-relation-6045455.title: Tiree Music Festival
osm-relation-6045455.summary: Tiree Music Festival is a Scottish folk music festival held annually on the Island of Tiree in the Inner Hebrides. The festival was founded in 2010 by resident Stewart MacLennan and local musician Daniel Gillespie of the band Skerryvore.
osm-relation-6045455.tie: Tiree Music Festival is a Scottish folk music festival held annually on the Island of Tiree in the Inner Hebrides. The festival was founded in 2010 by resident Stewart MacLennan and local musician Daniel Gillespie of the band Skerryvore.

osm-relation-4619204.title: Isle of Jura Fell Race
osm-relation-4619204.summary: The Isle of Jura Fell Race is an annual fell race held in May, starting and finishing at Craighouse on the Scottish island of Jura. The course loops west and north over several hills including the Paps of Jura.
osm-relation-4619204.tie: The Isle of Jura Fell Race is an annual fell race held in May, starting and finishing at Craighouse on the Scottish island of Jura. The course loops west and north over several hills including the Paps of Jura.

osm-relation-12658664.title: Yoal
osm-relation-12658664.summary: The yoal (Shaetlan pronunciation: [joɐɫ] YOHL), often referred to as the ness yoal, is a clinker-built craft used traditionally in Shetland, Scotland. Ian Best of Fair Isle, and Tommy Isbister of Trondra, are contemporary yoal builders.
osm-relation-12658664.tie: The yoal (Shaetlan pronunciation: [joɐɫ] YOHL), often referred to as the ness yoal, is a clinker-built craft used traditionally in Shetland, Scotland. Ian Best of Fair Isle, and Tommy Isbister of Trondra, are contemporary yoal builders.

osm-relation-6045364.title: Currach
osm-relation-6045364.summary: A currach (Irish: curach [ˈkʊɾˠəx]) is a type of Irish boat with a wooden frame, over which animal skins or hides were once stretched, though now canvas is more usual. In Achill Island the currach is built with double gunwales.
osm-relation-6045364.tie: A currach (Irish: curach [ˈkʊɾˠəx]) is a type of Irish boat with a wooden frame, over which animal skins or hides were once stretched, though now canvas is more usual. In Achill Island the currach is built with double gunwales.

osm-way-495525351.title: Curling-stone quarry
osm-way-495525351.summary: The island's microgranite has long been quarried to make curling stones. Ailsa Craig produced two types of granite for curling, Blue Hone and Ailsa Craig Common Green.
osm-way-495525351.tie: The island's microgranite has long been quarried to make curling stones. Ailsa Craig produced two types of granite for curling, Blue Hone and Ailsa Craig Common Green.

osm-relation-6046655.title: King of Bardsey
osm-relation-6046655.summary: Bardsey Island (Welsh: Ynys Enlli), known as the legendary "Island of 20,000 Saints", is located 1.9 miles (3.1 km) off the Llŷn Peninsula in the Welsh county of Gwynedd. It was tradition for the island to elect the "King of Bardsey" (Welsh: Brenin Enlli), and from 1826 onwards, he would be crowned by Baron Newborough or his representative.
osm-relation-6046655.tie: Bardsey Island (Welsh: Ynys Enlli), known as the legendary "Island of 20,000 Saints", is located 1.9 miles (3.1 km) off the Llŷn Peninsula in the Welsh county of Gwynedd. It was tradition for the island to elect the "King of Bardsey" (Welsh: Brenin Enlli), and from 1826 onwards, he would be crowned by Baron Newborough or his representative.

osm-relation-6045499.title: Fetlar sheepdog trials
osm-relation-6045499.summary: Fetlar is one of the North Isles of Shetland, Scotland, with a usually resident population of 61 at the time of the 2011 census and 66 in 2022. The Fetlar sheepdog trials take place annually, normally in July.
osm-relation-6045499.tie: Fetlar is one of the North Isles of Shetland, Scotland, with a usually resident population of 61 at the time of the 2011 census and 66 in 2022. The Fetlar sheepdog trials take place annually, normally in July.

osm-relation-6045499.title: Fetlar Foy
osm-relation-6045499.summary: The Fetlar Foy, once very popular with Shetlanders and tourists alike, took place at midsummer on the Links at Tresta where folk were entertained with music, food and drink.
osm-relation-6045499.tie: The Fetlar Foy, once very popular with Shetlanders and tourists alike, took place at midsummer on the Links at Tresta where folk were entertained with music, food and drink.

osm-way-4004501.title: Boat names on the cliff
osm-way-4004501.summary: As boats come into Canna harbour, names appear painted up the cliff behind the pier: fishing boats, their numbers, and home ports, refreshed by crews who call often. A published account of the cliff says the names are a visitors' book the boats keep themselves. One family has repainted their launch, Patrice, on visits since the 1950s.

image.note: Names painted on the cliff at Canna harbour
image.alt: Names painted on the cliff at Canna harbour

osm-way-172479890.title: Forvik declared independent
osm-way-172479890.summary: In June 2008 Stuart Hill declared the Shetland islet of Forvik a crown dependency and said it owed no allegiance to any United Kingdom government. Reuters reported the declaration the day it was made. Britain does not recognise the claim.

image.note: Forvik, the Shetland islet in the declaration
image.alt: Forvik, the Shetland islet in the declaration

wd-Q13706.title: Principality of Sealand
wd-Q13706.summary: In 1967 Roy Bates declared the abandoned wartime fort HM Fort Roughs, about seven miles off Suffolk, the Principality of Sealand. Marking fifty years of the claim, the BBC described a flag, a constitution, and passports. Britain does not recognise the principality.

image.note: HM Fort Roughs, the fort called Sealand
image.alt: HM Fort Roughs, the fort called Sealand

lundy.title: The puffin coins
lundy.summary: Martin Coles Harman, who bought Lundy in 1925, told the High Court in 1931 that he was sovereign of the island and entitled to issue puffin coins with his own head on them. Time reported that the court kept a fine under the Coinage Act and treated Lundy as part of the United Kingdom.

osm-relation-2324897.title: Declared free of anthrax
osm-relation-2324897.summary: Wartime anthrax tests left Gruinard Island closed for 48 years. On 24 April 1990 a defence minister crossed from the mainland, took down the red warning sign, and declared the island safe. The Herald reported the day.

osm-relation-2324897.title: Fire on the anthrax island
osm-relation-2324897.summary: In March 2022 a fire burned from one end of Gruinard Island to the other. The BBC reported the blaze on the uninhabited island, used for anthrax tests in the Second World War and declared clear in April 1990. The fire service said the empty island was outside its remit.

flannan-isles-eilean-mor-6-others.title: The keepers vanished
flannan-isles-eilean-mor-6-others.summary: On 15 December 1900 the three keepers of the Flannan Isles lighthouse vanished from Eilean Mòr. A relief crew landed on 26 December and found the light ready, the beds empty, and the last notes from that morning. In June 2026 the BBC reported that the letter the first keeper ashore wrote would go on public display.

osm-way-4569195.title: A new breed of cattle
osm-way-4569195.summary: The last residents left Swona in 1974 and the cattle stayed. In 1999 the BBC reported that the herd had bred without people for long enough to be entered as its own breed, the first new British cattle breed recognised in more than a century.

osm-way-4569195.title: Trainers in the post
osm-way-4569195.summary: In September 2025 a parcel addressed to Swona arrived in the post: a pair of trainers, for an island whose only inhabitants are feral cattle. The BBC reported that the people who look after Swona from South Ronaldsay did not know the name on the label, and that the island has no internet from which anyone there could have ordered them.

image.note: The cattle that live on Swona
image.alt: The cattle that live on Swona

osm-way-128077107.title: Prince of the Saltees
osm-way-128077107.summary: Michael Neale bought Great Saltee in 1943 and styled himself Prince of the Saltees. The Irish Times records that he set a throne and an obelisk on the island, and that his coronation was held there in 1953. As a boy he had told his mother he would one day own the island and be its prince.

osm-relation-1663615.title: The People's Republic of Eigg
osm-relation-1663615.summary: In 1997 the residents of Eigg bought their island after years of dispute with absentee landlords. A BBC account of that purchase calls it the moment a People's Republic of Eigg declared independence.

image.note: Galmisdale and An Sgùrr on Eigg
image.alt: Galmisdale and An Sgùrr on Eigg

osm-relation-1663615.title: A jog over a stegosaur
osm-relation-1663615.summary: A researcher jogging the foreshore of Eigg ran over a bone set in a boulder, the first dinosaur fossil found on the island. The Press and Journal reported a piece about a foot long, about 166 million years old, from the hind limb of a stegosaur.

mull.title: The night flight
mull.summary: On Christmas Eve 1975 Peter Gibbs took off alone, at night, from Glenforsa airfield on Mull and did not return. The BBC records that his body was found four months later on a hillside about a mile from the hotel, with no seawater on his clothes, and that the light aircraft was not with him.

osm-relation-14940656.title: Castaway
osm-relation-14940656.summary: In 2000 the BBC put 36 strangers on Taransay for a year and filmed them trying to build a community from scratch. By New Year seven had left, after gales that wrecked shelters they had built, a meningitis scare, and rows in public.

rockall.title: Forty days on the rock
rockall.summary: In 1985 Tom McClean spent 40 days and nights on Rockall, living in a wooden box bolted to the rock. He told the BBC he raised a Union flag when he landed and that he was the first person to reside there. Britain had annexed the rock in 1955.

fair-isle.title: The observatory burned
fair-isle.summary: On 10 March 2019 a fire destroyed the Fair Isle Bird Observatory. The BBC reported that extra crews had to be flown from Sumburgh and brought by boat, and that the smoke could be seen from the Shetland mainland. A family in the adjoining flat got out unhurt.

image.note: The Fair Isle observatory before the 2019 fire
image.alt: The Fair Isle observatory before the 2019 fire

osm-way-3099422.title: Crowned with beer
osm-way-3099422.summary: Whoever takes the Ship Inn on Piel Island is crowned king or queen, and the ceremony pours a jug of beer over their head. In 2025 the BBC met the landlord, Aaron Sanderson, who said he was crowned at 33 when he took the pub. He is recorded as the island's 24th king.

wd-Q38252228.title: Graves in the mud
wd-Q38252228.summary: Deadman's Island, a closed mudbank in the Swale opposite Queenborough, holds unmarked graves of people who died on prison hulks more than 200 years ago. In 2017 the BBC reported that erosion was washing those coffins out of the mud. The public are not allowed on the island.

image.note: Deadman's Island in the Swale. Not a photograph of the graves.
image.alt: Deadman's Island in the Swale. Not a photograph of the graves.

osm-way-2956937.title: The last feudal election
osm-way-2956937.summary: On 10 December 2008 Sark held its first fully democratic election in nearly 450 years and ended a feudal parliament. After candidates backed by the Barclay brothers lost, the Guardian reported that the brothers closed the shops, hotels, and building work they ran on the island, and that about 140 people lost their jobs.

osm-relation-15708714.title: Whisky from the wreck
osm-relation-15708714.summary: On 5 February 1941 the cargo ship SS Politician ran aground off Eriskay with about 250,000 bottles of whisky in the hold. The BBC's account says islanders rowed out and took cases ashore, and that Customs and Excise pursued them because no duty had been paid on the spirits.

image.note: Eriskay, where the SS Politician went aground
image.alt: Eriskay, where the SS Politician went aground

osm-relation-380646.title: The beach is the runway
osm-relation-380646.summary: Scheduled flights to Barra land on Tràigh Mhòr, a cockle beach at the north of the island, and the timetable follows the tide. The BBC describes it as the only beach runway in the world used for scheduled airline services. When the windsocks are down, the sand is a public beach again.

image.note: The cockle strand on Barra, used as the runway
image.alt: The cockle strand on Barra, used as the runway

st-kilda.title: The last boats
st-kilda.summary: On the morning of 29 August 1930 the last 36 people living on St Kilda left Hirta aboard HMS Harebell. The National Trust for Scotland records that they had asked the government that May to help them leave, because too few remained to keep the island through another winter.

image.note: Village Bay on Hirta, St Kilda
image.alt: Village Bay on Hirta, St Kilda

osm-relation-3148465.title: Scotland's earliest face
osm-relation-3148465.summary: In 2009 archaeologists at the Links of Noltland on Westray lifted a sandstone figurine a few centimetres tall from the mud of a Neolithic house. The BBC reported it as the earliest human face known from Scotland. It has come to be called the Westray Wife.

image.note: The sandstone figurine found on Westray
image.alt: The sandstone figurine found on Westray

osm-way-4569530.title: Two minutes in the air
osm-way-4569530.summary: The scheduled flight between Westray and Papa Westray covers 1.7 miles. The BBC reported that the hop takes about two minutes, including taxiing, and that the fastest recorded time was 53 seconds.

osm-relation-12597195.title: The beast on the rocks
osm-relation-12597195.summary: In September 1808 a carcass the islanders did not recognise washed onto the rocks at Rothiesholm Head on Stronsay. Witnesses put it at about 55 feet. The BBC, reporting later research, said some experts took it for a dead basking shark, while the drawings were compared with descriptions of the Loch Ness monster.

image.attribution: No machine-readable author provided. Islandhopper assumed (based on copyright claims).

osm-relation-12597195.title: A walrus under the ramp
osm-relation-12597195.summary: In April 2026 the pier master on Stronsay saw a walrus as the ferry came in, and it settled under the linkspan. The Orcadian called it the third walrus to turn up in Orkney in recent years.

image.attribution: No machine-readable author provided. Islandhopper assumed (based on copyright claims).

osm-relation-2797155.title: The raiders
osm-relation-2797155.summary: In July 1906 landless men from Barra, who the BBC says were not allowed to build a proper house there, took land on Vatersay. By 1909 the Congested Districts Board had bought the island and divided it into 58 crofts.

osm-way-495525351.title: Stones for the Olympics
osm-way-495525351.summary: The granite for the curling stones used at the Olympics is taken from Ailsa Craig, an uninhabited island in the Firth of Clyde. The BBC reported that one Ayrshire workshop has made them for more than 170 years, and that the rock is cut from the island about once a decade.

osm-relation-4619204.title: Caught in the whirlpool
osm-relation-4619204.summary: In 1947, while he was on Jura writing his last novel, George Orwell's boat was caught in the Corryvreckan whirlpool between Jura and Scarba. The BBC records that the outboard motor was torn off, the boat capsized, and Orwell got his young son onto the rocks of Eilean Mòr before a passing fisherman took them off.

image.note: The Corryvreckan, off the north of Jura
image.alt: The Corryvreckan, off the north of Jura

osm-relation-8609288.title: The car over the sound
osm-relation-8609288.summary: Ireland's only cable car runs from the Beara peninsula across open water to Dursey Island. RTÉ reported that it first opened on 5 December 1969, and that it reopened in June 2023 after the towers and ropes were replaced. The car carries six people.

image.note: The cable car to Dursey Island
image.alt: The cable car to Dursey Island

osm-relation-6045406.title: The furnished bus shelter
osm-relation-6045406.summary: After the bus shelter past Baltasound was taken away, a child wrote to the paper in 1996 asking for it back. The Shetland Times later described a sofa, a television, a heater and a carpet inside the replacement, and a website the British Library chose to archive. The shelter stands on Unst.

osm-relation-3148464.title: Two huts became a chapel
osm-relation-3148464.summary: Italian prisoners of war, held while they built the Churchill Barriers, made a chapel on Lamb Holm out of two Nissen huts. The Orcadian records Camp 60 on Lamb Holm as the place that chapel was built.

image.note: The Italian Chapel on Lamb Holm
image.alt: The Italian Chapel on Lamb Holm

osm-relation-6045499.title: A Viking hilt from the hill
osm-relation-6045499.summary: Shetland Museum took in a five-lobed sword pommel dated to about 900 to 1100, found on Fetlar. The Shetland Times reported the curator calling that kind of Viking find rare, and likely a status piece rather than a weapon that had been used.

osm-relation-380684.title: A funeral for a mermaid
osm-relation-380684.summary: The Stornoway Gazette retells an 1830 account from the west of Benbecula: a small body, described as human above and fish below, washed ashore near Nunton and was buried as a mermaid. The paper says no grave has been found.

osm-relation-6045516.title: Three bears on the beach
osm-relation-6045516.summary: In 2016 three hairy carcasses washed up at different points on the west coast of Colonsay, and people on the island took them for polar bears. The Press and Journal reported that the Royal Zoological Society of Scotland called a polar bear highly unlikely.

osm-relation-1663893.title: A road built by one man
osm-relation-1663893.summary: In 1964, after the council would not build a road in the north of Raasay, Calum MacLeod started the stretch from Brochel to Arnish himself. The Press and Journal says he worked into the mid-1970s with a shovel, a pick and a wheelbarrow.

image.attribution: No machine-readable author provided. Imamon~commonswiki assumed (based on copyright claims).

lewis-and-harris.title: Chessmen in a sand dune
lewis-and-harris.summary: The Stornoway Gazette records that the Lewis chessmen were found in 1831 in a small stone cist in a sand dune at Uig. Most of the pieces are carved from walrus tusk.

isle-of-skye.title: Plaster in the footprints
isle-of-skye.summary: Police on Skye investigated damage to dinosaur footprints at Staffin that are about 165 million years old. The Press and Journal reported that plaster had been poured into two of the prints.

image.note: An Corran beach at Staffin, Skye
image.alt: An Corran beach at Staffin, Skye

osm-relation-1240445.title: The last post on Tanera
osm-relation-1240445.summary: The Press and Journal reported that the last permanent residents had left Tanera Mòr, the last inhabited of the Summer Isles. The sale included a private postal service and a licence to design the island's own stamps, and 2014 was the first year in more than fifteen with no new issue.

osm-relation-6045364.title: A henge built over a weekend
osm-relation-6045364.summary: On 25 November 2011 more than thirty lorries arrived on Achill with concrete, and by Sunday a circle about 30 metres across stood on a hillside above Pollagh. The Mayo News reported that two years later the circle was still there, after the courts had ordered it taken down.

osm-way-329053691.title: Wallabies that were meant to fade
osm-way-329053691.summary: Red-necked wallabies have lived on Lambay, off Dublin, for more than fifty years, starting with a small group brought in the 1950s. Newstalk reported that the hope had been they would die out quietly, and that the estimate was now more than 500.

osm-way-128067375.title: Tunnels under the fort
osm-way-128067375.summary: The Irish Examiner reported hundreds of metres of tunnels under the old punishment block on Spike Island, with storerooms the managers had not expected. A 16th-century smugglers' tunnel on the island is known as well, and its entrance has been covered until it can be surveyed.

image.note: The entrance to Fort Mitchel on Spike Island
image.alt: The entrance to Fort Mitchel on Spike Island

osm-relation-3235264.title: The crew came ashore in a buoy
osm-relation-3235264.summary: On Inis Oírr, the wreck of the Plassey sits on the shore as a landmark. The Irish Times records that in 1960 a breeches buoy brought the whole crew off the ship and onto the island.

osm-relation-7230308.title: A wire under the Atlantic
osm-relation-7230308.summary: The first telegraph cable under the Atlantic ran from Valentia Island to Newfoundland. The Irish Examiner records that a cable laid in 1858 failed within a month, and that a new one was laid in July 1866, with a station on the island.

rathlin.title: The lamp at the bottom
rathlin.summary: Rathlin West Light was built into the cliff and first lit on 10 March 1919. The Irish News calls it Ireland's only upside-down lighthouse, because the lamp sits at the bottom so the beam can shine under the low fog.

image.note: The cliff by Rathlin West Light

osm-way-1493515027.title: Carcasses with legs
osm-way-1493515027.summary: In November 1953 a carcass more than two feet long, with leg-like fins, washed up on Canvey Island. Essex Live records a second, larger one on the same shore in August 1954, and says the likely identification now is an angler fish.

osm-way-1493746453.title: The monkeys came down to the beach
osm-way-1493746453.summary: In 1968 a zoo was opened in the fort on St Catherine's Island, the tidal rock off Tenby. Wales Online reported that the monkeys later got out, climbed down to the beach, and made off with hats and bags.

scilly-st-marys.title: The containers came ashore
scilly-st-marys.summary: At 3am on 26 March 1997 the container ship Cita ran aground off St Mary's and the containers broke open along the south shore. Cornwall Live reported that people on the island carried off tyres, trainers, toys and blank gravestones.

osm-way-462551174.title: Two tropical birds on one rock
osm-way-462551174.summary: In August 2023 a red-footed booby, only the second recorded in Britain, was seen on Bishop Rock lighthouse. Cornwall Live reported that a brown booby was then found at the foot of the same light, and that having both tropical species there together was called extraordinary.

osm-way-1493651984.title: The wreck that left its rats
osm-way-1493651984.summary: On 15 March 1934 the steamship Herefordshire, under tow to a breaker's yard, broke her ropes and came ashore on Cardigan Island. Wales Online reported that rats from the wreck then wiped out the island's puffins, and that the rats were not cleared for more than forty-five years.

osm-relation-6046655.title: A king crowned on a chair
osm-relation-6046655.summary: Bardsey had its own kings from about 1796 until the last died in 1926. North Wales Live describes a crowning held outdoors on the island, the new king stood on a chair, with boats lying offshore.

osm-way-126546636.title: A cholera ward in the channel
osm-way-126546636.summary: From 1883 Flat Holm was used as an isolation hospital for cholera brought in by ships. Wales Online records a permanent hospital built there in 1896, and that the Ministry of Health condemned the building in 1935.

brownsea.title: Leprosy in the squirrels
brownsea.summary: Post-mortem examinations found leprosy in red squirrels on Brownsea Island, and a study was set up there to learn how it spreads. The Bournemouth Echo reported that only a few of the island's squirrels were ill, and that the risk to people was described as very small.

osm-relation-12913146.title: A blonde mole on the runway
osm-relation-12913146.summary: A blonde mole, about one in ten thousand, turned up while moles were being cleared from Alderney's grass runway. The Jersey Evening Post reported that the animal was leucistic, with brown eyes, rather than an albino.
